**Top 5 cancers causing the most deaths among women worldwide (2020 – the latest GLOBOCAN/WHO dataset)**  

| Rank | Cancer (female) | Approx. number of deaths in 2020* |
|------|----------------|-----------------------------------|
| 1 | **Breast cancer** | **≈ 685 000** deaths |
| 2 | **Lung (tracheal, bronchial, and lung) cancer** | **≈ 493 000** deaths |
| 3 | **Stomach (gastric) cancer** | **≈ 312 000** deaths |
| 4 | **Colorectal (colon & rectum) cancer** | **≈ 280 000** deaths |
| 5 | **Liver cancer** | **≈ 236 000** deaths |

\*Numbers are rounded estimates taken from the **GLOBOCAN 2020** database (International Agency for Research on Cancer – IARC), which is the most recent WHO‑approved global cancer‑mortality compilation covering the period 2020.  The figures represent deaths **among females only** (the database provides sex‑specific mortality).

### Why these cancers rank highest

| Cancer | Why it drives female mortality globally |
|--------|------------------------------------------|
| **Breast** | By far the most common cancer in women; high incidence in both high‑ and middle‑income countries, and despite advances in early detection, many cases are diagnosed at later stages in low‑resource settings. |
| **Lung** | Smoking prevalence among women has risen in many regions (especially East Asia and parts of Europe). Even where smoking rates are lower, indoor air pollution and occupational exposures contribute. |
| **Stomach** | Historically high in East Asia (China, Japan, Korea) and parts of Latin America; infection with *Helicobacter pylori* remains a major risk factor, and screening is limited in many high‑burden countries. |
| **Colorectal** | Incidence is climbing worldwide as diets become more “Westernized” (high red‑meat, low fibre) and obesity rises; screening programs are unevenly implemented, leading to later‑stage diagnoses in many regions. |
| **Liver** | Chronic infection with hepatitis B and C, aflatoxin exposure, and rising rates of non‑alcoholic fatty liver disease (linked to obesity/diabetes) drive mortality, especially in East Asia and sub‑Saharan Africa. |

### Sources

1. **IARC GLOBOCAN 2020** – “Cancer Fact Sheets” (sex‑specific mortality tables).  
   *URL (accessed 2025‑11‑01):* https://gco.iarc.fr/today/data/factsheets/cancers  
2. **World Health Organization (WHO)** – “Global Health Estimates 2020” – used for cross‑validation of total cancer‑death numbers.  
   *URL:* https://www.who.int/data/gho/data/themes/topics/topic-details/GHO/cancer-mortality  

These sources are the authoritative references for worldwide cancer incidence and mortality and are updated periodically; the 2020 edition is the most recent complete release, with 2021‑2022 provisional updates still pending.

• Pronounced jaundice, dark urine, pale stools
• Ascites (abdominal swelling due to fluid)
• Upper‑body bruising/bleeding (coagulopathy)
• Metastatic symptoms (bone pain, lung symptoms) | ### Quick Reference Checklist (for patients & clinicians) - **New lump, skin changes, nipple discharge** → think **breast**. - **Persistent cough, blood in sputum, unexplained breathlessness** → think **lung**. - **Early satiety, upper‑abdominal pain, melena** → think **stomach**. - **Bowel habit change, blood/mucus in stool, abdominal cramps** → think **colorectal**. - **Right‑upper‑quadrant fullness, jaundice, rapid weight loss** → think **liver**. > **Note:** Many of these cancers can be asymptomatic in early stages; screening (mammography, low‑dose CT for high‑risk smokers, colonoscopy, H. pylori testing, hepatitis B/C vaccination/screening) remains crucial for early detection and improving survival. --- ### Sources 1. **IARC GLOBOCAN 2020** – “Cancer Fact Sheets” (sex‑specific mortality tables). *URL (accessed 2025‑11‑01):* https://gco.iarc.fr/today/data/factsheets/cancers 2. **World Health Organization (WHO)** – Global Health Estimates 2020 (cancer mortality validation). *URL:* https://www.who.int/data/gho/data/themes/topics/topic-details/GHO/cancer-mortality 3.
